fields.Question:
Crawler workers share a thread safe set. Two workers sometimes fetch the same URL. What is the fix?
if url not in visited:
    visited.add(url)
    fetch(url)
fields.Choices:
Use a thread safe set, since its individual operations are already atomic
Mark visited as volatile so every worker sees the latest contents
Fetch first and add to visited afterwards so only successful URLs are recorded
Make the check and the add one atomic step, such as add returning whether it inserted, or a lock around both
fields.Correct: Make the check and the add one atomic step, such as add returning whether it inserted, or a lock around both
fields.Explanation: Each set call is atomic, but the gap between contains and add is not: both workers can see the URL missing and both proceed. An atomic insert that reports whether it won (putIfAbsent, add returning a boolean, or a lock covering both calls) closes the window. The thread safe set alone is exactly the code shown, so the race stays. Visibility (volatile) does not make two operations one. Adding after the fetch widens the race window instead of closing it.
fields.Hint: Two safe calls in a row are not one safe call.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Multithreaded web crawler (https://www.hellointerview.com/community/questions/web-crawler-multithreaded/cm5eguhad02yw838ot9p159t6)
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: A multithreaded crawler uses a shared queue of URLs and N workers. When should the crawl be declared finished?
fields.Choices:
As soon as the queue is empty
When every worker has been idle for a fixed timeout, such as 5 seconds
When the queue is empty and no worker is still processing a page
When the visited set stops growing between two checks
fields.Correct: When the queue is empty and no worker is still processing a page
fields.Explanation: A worker that is mid fetch can still discover and enqueue new URLs, so an empty queue alone is not the end. Track pending work (queued plus in flight) under a lock or an atomic counter and finish when it hits zero. Stopping on an empty queue exits early whenever the queue briefly drains. A timeout guesses and breaks on a slow host. A visited set that did not grow between two samples says nothing about pages still being fetched.
fields.Hint: Work in flight can create more work.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Multithreaded web crawler (https://www.hellointerview.com/community/questions/web-crawler-multithreaded/cm5eguhad02yw838ot9p159t6)
LeetCode 1242: Web Crawler Multithreaded (https://leetcode.com/problems/web-crawler-multithreaded/)

fields.Question: Crawler workers decrement a shared pending counter after finishing a page, and the coordinator stops when pending is 0. When must a worker increment pending for each new link it finds?
fields.Choices:
After it decrements pending for the page it just finished
Before it decrements pending for the page it just finished
Only after the new link has been fetched successfully
It does not matter as long as the counter is atomic
fields.Correct: Before it decrements pending for the page it just finished
fields.Explanation: If the worker decrements first, pending can momentarily reach 0 while new links are known but not yet counted, and the coordinator stops early. Incrementing for children first keeps pending above zero for as long as any work exists. Decrementing first is exactly the early exit bug. Counting only after a fetch means unfetched links are invisible to termination. An atomic counter makes each update safe but does not fix the ordering between two updates.
fields.Hint: Can the counter hit zero while work still exists?
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Multithreaded web crawler (https://www.hellointerview.com/community/questions/web-crawler-multithreaded/cm5eguhad02yw838ot9p159t6)
LeetCode 1242: Web Crawler Multithreaded (https://leetcode.com/problems/web-crawler-multithreaded/)

fields.Question: A crawler must fetch about 10 million pages with at most 64 concurrent requests on one machine. Which design fits?
fields.Choices:
A fixed pool of 64 workers pulling from a shared frontier queue
Start one new thread for every discovered URL
Start one new thread per page but sleep between thread starts
Fetch all links of a page in parallel with no limit, then recurse
fields.Correct: A fixed pool of 64 workers pulling from a shared frontier queue
fields.Explanation: A fixed pool caps concurrency at exactly the limit and reuses threads, and the frontier queue absorbs bursts of discovered links. A thread per URL creates millions of threads, exhausts memory and file descriptors and blows past the request limit. Sleeping between starts only slows creation; the number alive is still unbounded when fetches are slow. Unbounded fan out per page has the same problem recursively.
fields.Hint: Bound the workers, not the work.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Multithreaded web crawler (https://www.hellointerview.com/community/questions/web-crawler-multithreaded/cm5eguhad02yw838ot9p159t6)
interviewing.io: Anthropic interview questions (https://interviewing.io/anthropic-interview-questions)

fields.Question: A concurrent crawler with 64 workers must send at most one request per second to each host, and most frontier URLs belong to a few hosts. Which design keeps the workers busy while obeying the limit?
fields.Choices:
One global lock held by a worker while it sleeps one second after each request
One global rate limiter of 64 requests per second
Each worker sleeps one second after every request
Per host queues with a next allowed time, and workers pick any host whose time has passed
fields.Correct: Per host queues with a next allowed time, and workers pick any host whose time has passed
fields.Explanation: Per host queues let a worker skip hosts that are cooling down and fetch from hosts that are ready, so the rule holds per host without idling the pool. A global lock held across a sleep serialises the whole crawler to one request per second total. A global rate is not a per host limit and can hit one host 64 times a second. Per worker sleeps do not coordinate across workers, so 64 workers can still hit the same host 64 times a second.
fields.Hint: The limit is per host, so the state should be per host.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Multithreaded web crawler (https://www.hellointerview.com/community/questions/web-crawler-multithreaded/cm5eguhad02yw838ot9p159t6)
IGotAnOffer: OpenAI coding interview (https://igotanoffer.com/en/advice/openai-coding-interview)

fields.Question: You wrote a single threaded crawler (BFS from a start URL, same host only). The interviewer asks you to make it concurrent. Talk through the changes.
fields.Answer:
Keep the BFS shape, then change four things.

Workers: a fixed pool sized for I/O (tens of workers, or an async loop with a semaphore), pulling from a shared frontier queue.

Dedup: an atomic insert into visited (putIfAbsent or a lock around check and add) done when a URL is enqueued, not when it is fetched.

Termination: a pending counter: increment for each new URL before decrementing for the finished one, and stop when it reaches zero; then send poison pills or close the queue so workers exit.

Failure handling: timeouts per fetch, a retry limit, and an exception in one fetch must still decrement pending.

Follow ups: per host politeness, bounded frontier for memory, and measuring the speedup against the single threaded version.
fields.Hint: Pool, atomic dedup, termination, errors.
fields.Fact: The hard parts are atomic dedup and knowing when you are done.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Multithreaded web crawler (https://www.hellointerview.com/community/questions/web-crawler-multithreaded/cm5eguhad02yw838ot9p159t6)
interviewing.io: Anthropic interview questions (https://interviewing.io/anthropic-interview-questions)
IGotAnOffer: OpenAI coding interview (https://igotanoffer.com/en/advice/openai-coding-interview)

fields.Question: The concurrent crawler now needs to run on 100 machines. How do you partition work and dedup URLs across them?
fields.Answer:
Partition by host: hash the host to pick the owning machine, so politeness and robots state stay local and each machine dedups its own URLs.

Routing: a machine that finds a link it does not own sends it to the owner through a queue (Kafka or RPC batches).

Dedup: the owner keeps the visited set, in memory with a Bloom filter in front, or in a shared key value store if machines are stateless.

Failure: consistent hashing so a lost machine moves only its share, and the frontier persisted so work is not lost.

Termination: a global pending count is expensive, so most real crawlers run continuously and track freshness rather than detecting a global end.
fields.Hint: Who owns a URL?
fields.Fact: Hash by host: politeness and dedup become local problems.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Multithreaded web crawler (https://www.hellointerview.com/community/questions/web-crawler-multithreaded/cm5eguhad02yw838ot9p159t6)
IGotAnOffer: OpenAI coding interview (https://igotanoffer.com/en/advice/openai-coding-interview)

fields.Question:
A consumer waits like this on a shared queue with several consumers. What bug can it cause?
lock.acquire()
if queue.empty():
    not_empty.wait()
item = queue.pop()
lock.release()
fields.Choices:
After waking, the queue can be empty again, so pop fails; the check must be a while loop
None, because wait reacquires the lock before returning
A deadlock, because wait does not release the lock
Lost notifications, because notify can fire before wait is called
fields.Correct: After waking, the queue can be empty again, so pop fails; the check must be a while loop
fields.Explanation: Wait releases the lock and reacquires it on return, but between the notify and the reacquire another consumer can take the item, and spurious wakeups are allowed by POSIX. Only a while loop re-checks the predicate. Reacquiring the lock is true but does not make the state still valid. Wait does release the lock, so it does not deadlock. Lost notifications are prevented here because the predicate is checked under the lock before waiting.
fields.Hint: Who else could run between notify and your wakeup?
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Condition Variables (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-cv.pdf)
pthread_cond_wait, The Open Group Base Specifications (https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_cond_wait.html)

fields.Question: A bounded queue uses one condition variable for both producers and consumers, and calls notify (wake one) after each put and get. What can happen?
fields.Choices:
Nothing, one condition is enough as long as waits use while loops
Items are delivered out of order
Producers can overflow the capacity
A producer can wake another producer instead of a consumer, and everyone ends up waiting
fields.Correct: A producer can wake another producer instead of a consumer, and everyone ends up waiting
fields.Explanation: With one shared condition, notify may wake a thread of the same kind, which re-checks, goes back to sleep, and the wakeup meant for the other side is lost; all threads can end up asleep. Use two conditions (not_full and not_empty) or notify_all. While loops prevent wrong progress but not this stall. Ordering is decided by the queue, not the notifications. Capacity is protected by the while check, so overflow does not happen.
fields.Hint: Which kind of thread does notify wake?
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Condition Variables (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-cv.pdf)
LeetCode 1188: Design Bounded Blocking Queue (https://leetcode.com/problems/design-bounded-blocking-queue/)

fields.Question: In a correct bounded queue, which state change must happen while holding the mutex associated with the condition variable?
fields.Choices:
Calling notify, otherwise the wakeup is ignored
Nothing, the condition variable makes the queue thread safe
Changing the queue contents that the waiters' predicate reads
Only the wait call; updates can happen outside the lock
fields.Correct: Changing the queue contents that the waiters' predicate reads
fields.Explanation: The predicate state (queue length) must be updated under the same mutex the waiter holds while checking it; otherwise a waiter can check, miss the update, and sleep forever. POSIX allows signalling with or without the mutex held, so notify outside the lock is not itself the bug (some libraries like Python require holding it, but that is an API rule). A condition variable is only a wait queue and protects nothing. Updates outside the lock reintroduce the lost wakeup race.
fields.Hint: What does the waiter read before sleeping?
fields.Source:
pthread_cond_wait, The Open Group Base Specifications (https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_cond_wait.html)
OSTEP: Condition Variables (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-cv.pdf)

fields.Question: A semaphore based bounded buffer has empty (starts at N), full (starts at 0) and a mutex. Which put ordering is correct?
fields.Choices:
Lock mutex, wait on empty, insert, signal full, unlock mutex
Wait on empty, lock mutex, insert, unlock mutex, signal full
Wait on full, lock mutex, insert, unlock mutex, signal empty
Lock mutex, insert, unlock mutex, then wait on empty
fields.Correct: Wait on empty, lock mutex, insert, unlock mutex, signal full
fields.Explanation: The counting semaphore must be waited on before the mutex: a producer that blocks on empty while holding the mutex stops every consumer from freeing a slot, so all threads deadlock. Waiting on full in put inverts the roles of the two semaphores. Inserting before waiting on empty can overflow the buffer because the slot was never reserved.
fields.Hint: Never sleep on a semaphore while holding the mutex.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Semaphores (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-sema.pdf)

fields.Question: You add put(item, timeout) to a blocking queue. The wait can wake spuriously or lose the race for a free slot. How should the timeout be handled?
fields.Choices:
Compute a deadline once, and on each loop iteration wait only for the time remaining until it
Call wait(timeout) inside the while loop with the original timeout each time
Call wait(timeout) once with an if check, since a timeout cannot loop forever
Sleep for the timeout outside the lock, then check once
fields.Correct: Compute a deadline once, and on each loop iteration wait only for the time remaining until it
fields.Explanation: A deadline keeps the total wait bounded across repeated wakeups and still re-checks the predicate each time. Reusing the full timeout in a loop restarts the clock on every spurious or stolen wakeup, so the call can block far longer than requested. A single if wait brings back the stolen slot bug. Sleeping outside the lock wastes the full timeout even when a slot frees immediately, and the single check is still racy.
fields.Hint: The total time must stay bounded across wakeups.
fields.Source:
pthread_cond_wait, The Open Group Base Specifications (https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_cond_wait.html)
LeetCode 1188: Design Bounded Blocking Queue (https://leetcode.com/problems/design-bounded-blocking-queue/)

fields.Question: Consumers block in get() on an empty queue. You add close() so they exit cleanly. What must close do?
fields.Choices:
Set a closed flag without taking the lock, since a boolean write is atomic
Notify one waiter, since that waiter can wake the next
Interrupt or kill the consumer threads
Set a closed flag under the lock and notify all waiters, and get returns or raises when closed and empty
fields.Correct: Set a closed flag under the lock and notify all waiters, and get returns or raises when closed and empty
fields.Explanation: Waiters check the closed flag in their while predicate, so it must be set under the lock and every waiter must be woken with notify all; otherwise some stay asleep forever. An unlocked write can race with a waiter that checked the flag and is about to sleep, losing the wakeup. Chaining one notify relies on every consumer remembering to pass it on and breaks if any exits by another path. Killing threads skips cleanup and leaves locks and items in unknown states.
fields.Hint: Every sleeper needs to wake and see the flag.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Condition Variables (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-cv.pdf)
SpaceComplexity: Databricks onsite interview (https://spacecomplexity.ai/blog/databricks-onsite-interview)

fields.Question: A lock free ring buffer with one head and one tail index, each updated with plain atomic loads and stores, is correct for which setup?
fields.Choices:
Any number of producers and consumers
Many producers and one consumer
Exactly one producer and one consumer
One producer and many consumers
fields.Correct: Exactly one producer and one consumer
fields.Explanation: With one producer only it writes tail and with one consumer only it writes head, so each index has a single writer and loads and stores with release and acquire ordering are enough. With multiple producers two can read the same tail and write the same slot; with multiple consumers two can take the same item. Supporting those needs CAS on the indices or per slot sequence numbers.
fields.Hint: Who writes each index?
fields.Source:
What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory (https://people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdf)
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: You build a thread safe LRU cache from a concurrent hash map plus a linked list for recency. Is that enough?
fields.Choices:
Yes, the concurrent map makes the whole cache thread safe
No: get moves a node in the list, so map and list updates need one lock (or a design that batches recency updates)
Yes, if get takes a read lock and put takes a write lock
No, but making the list nodes volatile fixes it
fields.Correct: No: get moves a node in the list, so map and list updates need one lock (or a design that batches recency updates)
fields.Explanation: The invariant spans two structures: the map entry and the node position must change together, and get itself mutates recency. A concurrent map protects only map operations, so list reorders still race and corrupt the list. A read lock for get is wrong because get writes. Volatile only gives visibility of single fields, not atomic multi pointer updates. Real caches use one lock, striped segments, or buffered recency (as Caffeine does).
fields.Hint: Does get only read?
fields.Source:
Blind: Confusing experience of Databricks interview (https://www.teamblind.com/post/confusing-experience-of-databricks-interview-um6p8k8f)
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: When does replacing a mutex with a read write lock clearly help?
fields.Choices:
Many concurrent readers, rare writes, and read critical sections long enough to matter
Whenever reads outnumber writes at all
When writes are frequent and short
Always, because readers never block each other
fields.Correct: Many concurrent readers, rare writes, and read critical sections long enough to matter
fields.Explanation: A read write lock costs more per acquire than a mutex, so it only wins when many readers truly overlap and hold the lock long enough. A slight read majority with tiny critical sections is often slower than a plain mutex. Frequent writes serialise everything and can starve readers or writers. Readers do block when a writer is waiting or holding the lock, so it is not free.
fields.Hint: The lock itself has a cost.
fields.Source:
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)
OSTEP: Locks (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-locks.pdf)

fields.Question: Two threads each hold the read lock of a non upgradable read write lock and both try to acquire the write lock to update the entry they read. What happens?
fields.Choices:
One of them gets upgraded automatically
Both get the write lock in turn
The second one fails with an exception immediately
Deadlock: each waits for the other to release its read lock
fields.Correct: Deadlock: each waits for the other to release its read lock
fields.Explanation: A writer needs all readers gone, and each would be writer is itself a reader that will not let go, so both wait forever. Most read write locks (Java ReentrantReadWriteLock, pthread rwlock) do not upgrade. Release the read lock, take the write lock, and re-check the state, or use a lock with an explicit single upgrader mode.
fields.Hint: A writer needs zero readers.
fields.Source:
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)
OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)

fields.Question: A counter uses compare and swap: read v, compute v + 1, CAS(v, v + 1). What must happen when the CAS fails?
fields.Choices:
Retry the CAS with the same old value
Give up, since another thread already incremented it
Re-read the current value and retry the computation
Take a lock and write v + 1 directly
fields.Correct: Re-read the current value and retry the computation
fields.Explanation: CAS fails because the value changed, so the computation must restart from the fresh value. Retrying with the stale value fails every time, because the counter has already moved past it. Giving up loses this thread's increment. Writing v + 1 under a lock that other CAS users ignore overwrites concurrent updates.
fields.Hint: The old value is stale now.
fields.Source:
Blind: Confusing experience of Databricks interview (https://www.teamblind.com/post/confusing-experience-of-databricks-interview-um6p8k8f)
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: A lock free stack pops with CAS(head, old, old.next). Thread 1 reads old = A and A.next = B, then stalls. Others pop A, pop B, push A back. Thread 1 resumes. What happens?
fields.Choices:
The CAS fails because head changed twice
The CAS succeeds and head becomes B, a node that was already removed
The CAS succeeds and the stack is correct
The CAS spins forever
fields.Correct: The CAS succeeds and head becomes B, a node that was already removed
fields.Explanation: This is the ABA problem: CAS only compares the pointer, head is A again, so it succeeds and installs the stale next pointer B. Head changing in between is invisible to CAS. The result is corrupt because B was popped. Fixes are tagged pointers or version counters, hazard pointers, or garbage collected memory that prevents A from being reused while referenced.
fields.Hint: CAS compares values, not history.
fields.Source: Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: An in memory key value store with one global lock shows heavy contention on 32 cores, with operations spread across many keys. Which change reduces contention without breaking single key atomicity?
fields.Choices:
Lock striping: hash each key to one of many locks
Remove the lock, since each map operation is quick
Switch the global lock to a spinlock
Make the global lock a read write lock and take the read lock for puts
fields.Correct: Lock striping: hash each key to one of many locks
fields.Explanation: Striping lets operations on different keys proceed in parallel while each key is still guarded by exactly one lock. Removing the lock corrupts the map on concurrent resize or insert. A spinlock is still one global lock and burns CPU under contention. Taking a read lock for a write lets concurrent puts mutate the map at the same time.
fields.Hint: Spread the lock across keys.
fields.Source:
Blind: Confusing experience of Databricks interview (https://www.teamblind.com/post/confusing-experience-of-databricks-interview-um6p8k8f)
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: A striped key value store adds transfer(k1, k2) that must update both keys atomically. How should it lock?
fields.Choices:
Lock k1's stripe then k2's stripe in argument order
Lock each stripe only while updating that key
Lock k1's stripe and use try lock on k2's stripe, retrying immediately on failure
Lock both stripes in a fixed global order, such as by stripe index, skipping the second if equal
fields.Correct: Lock both stripes in a fixed global order, such as by stripe index, skipping the second if equal
fields.Explanation: Acquiring stripes in a global order makes cycles impossible, and checking for the same stripe avoids locking one non reentrant lock twice. Argument order deadlocks when one call does (a, b) and another (b, a). Locking separately lets readers see half a transfer. Immediate try lock retries avoid deadlock but can livelock under contention without backoff.
fields.Hint: Deadlock needs a cycle in lock order.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)
Blind: Confusing experience of Databricks interview (https://www.teamblind.com/post/confusing-experience-of-databricks-interview-um6p8k8f)

fields.Question: A shared counter is declared volatile (Java) or atomic load and store only. Two threads each run count = count + 1 a thousand times. What is the final value?
fields.Choices:
Always 2000, because volatile makes each access atomic
Always 1000, because writes overwrite each other
Anywhere up to 2000, because read and write are separate steps
Undefined, because volatile disables caching
fields.Correct: Anywhere up to 2000, because read and write are separate steps
fields.Explanation: Volatile guarantees visibility and ordering of each read and each write, but the read, add and write are three steps, so updates are lost when they interleave. Use an atomic increment or a lock. Always 2000 confuses visibility with atomicity. Always 1000 assumes perfect interleaving that rarely happens. Volatile does not turn off CPU caches; coherence handles that.
fields.Hint: Visibility is not atomicity.
fields.Source:
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)
OSTEP: Concurrency: An Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)

fields.Question: Design a thread safe LRU cache with per entry TTL that serves a hot read path on many cores. Walk through locking and expiry.
fields.Answer:
Baseline: hash map plus doubly linked list under one mutex; get moves to front, put inserts and evicts the tail, both O(1).

Expiry: store an expiry timestamp per entry and treat expired entries as misses on get (lazy), plus a background sweeper or a timer wheel to free memory for entries never read again.

Scaling reads: shard into N independent LRUs by key hash (approximate global LRU, much less contention), or record accesses in a per thread buffer and apply recency updates in batches under the lock.

Pitfalls: read lock for get (get writes), checking expiry outside the lock, and doing loads on miss while holding the lock (use a per key future so only one loader runs).
fields.Hint: Shard, lazy expiry, no I/O under the lock.
fields.Fact: Sharding trades exact LRU order for contention.
fields.Source:
Blind: Confusing experience of Databricks interview (https://www.teamblind.com/post/confusing-experience-of-databricks-interview-um6p8k8f)
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question:
A sliding window limiter allows 10 requests per second. Under load it lets through 12 in a second. What is the likely bug?
prune(log, now - 1s)
if len(log) < 10:
    log.append(now)
    return True
return False
fields.Choices:
The prune, count and append run without one lock, so several threads pass the check before any appends
The window should be 0.9 seconds to leave headroom
The log should be a set so duplicates are dropped
Clock skew between threads makes now inaccurate
fields.Correct: The prune, count and append run without one lock, so several threads pass the check before any appends
fields.Explanation: The decision reads the count and then writes it in separate steps; concurrent callers all see 9 and all append. The whole prune, check and append must be one critical section (or a CAS on a token count). Shrinking the window hides the race rather than fixing it. A set drops requests with equal timestamps, which miscounts. Threads on one machine share the same monotonic clock.
fields.Hint: Check then act again.
fields.Source:
Anthropic concurrency interview questions (https://www.linkjob.ai/interview-questions/anthropic-concurrency-interview/)
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: A token bucket for many keys needs to refill at r tokens per second. Which refill approach scales best?
fields.Choices:
A background thread per key that adds one token every 1/r seconds
One global timer thread that walks every key each millisecond
Reset the bucket to full at the start of each second
On each request, add (now minus last refill) times r, capped at capacity, then try to take a token
fields.Correct: On each request, add (now minus last refill) times r, capped at capacity, then try to take a token
fields.Explanation: Lazy refill computes tokens from elapsed time when needed, so idle keys cost nothing and no timers exist. A thread per key does not scale past a few thousand keys. A global sweep each millisecond is O(keys) work even when nothing happens. Resetting each second is a fixed window and allows 2x bursts across the boundary.
fields.Hint: Compute tokens from time, do not schedule them.
fields.Source: Anthropic concurrency interview questions (https://www.linkjob.ai/interview-questions/anthropic-concurrency-interview/)

fields.Question: A fixed window limiter allows 100 requests per minute, with the window reset on the minute. What is the most a client can send in any 60 second span?
fields.Choices:
100, since each window allows only 100
150, since bursts average out
200, by sending 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next
101, due to off by one at the boundary
fields.Correct: 200, by sending 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next
fields.Explanation: Two adjacent windows each allow 100 and nothing stops a client clustering them around the boundary, so a sliding 60 seconds can see 200. That is why sliding log, sliding window counter or token bucket are used when bursts matter. 100 assumes a sliding window. 150 and 101 are not derived from the rule.
fields.Hint: Look across the boundary.
fields.Source: Anthropic concurrency interview questions (https://www.linkjob.ai/interview-questions/anthropic-concurrency-interview/)

fields.Question: A limiter keeps a map from user id to sliding window state. Under load, one global lock is the bottleneck. Which design keeps per user decisions exact and removes the bottleneck?
fields.Choices:
Drop the lock and accept small overcounts
A concurrent map from user id to state, with a lock or atomic update per user entry
Keep one global lock but make the critical section only the append
Give each request thread its own copy of the map
fields.Correct: A concurrent map from user id to state, with a lock or atomic update per user entry
fields.Explanation: Users are independent, so per entry locking (computeIfAbsent then lock the entry, or a CAS on the entry) keeps each user's decision atomic while different users proceed in parallel. Dropping the lock lets bursts through and can corrupt the map. Shrinking the critical section to the append separates check from act, which is the race. Per thread maps let a user use the full limit on every thread.
fields.Hint: Users are independent of each other.
fields.Source:
Anthropic concurrency interview questions (https://www.linkjob.ai/interview-questions/anthropic-concurrency-interview/)
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: A CPU bound job (pure computation, no I/O) runs on an 8 core machine. Which approach gives near linear speedup in a runtime without a global interpreter lock?
fields.Choices:
About 8 workers (threads or processes), one per core
About 200 threads, since more threads hide latency
A single threaded async event loop
One thread, since context switching makes parallelism slower
fields.Correct: About 8 workers (threads or processes), one per core
fields.Explanation: CPU bound work scales with cores, so one worker per core keeps every core busy with minimal switching. Hundreds of threads add switching and cache pressure with no extra cores to run on. An event loop runs on one core and only helps when tasks wait on I/O. Context switching costs little at 8 workers on 8 cores.
fields.Hint: What is the bottleneck resource?
fields.Source:
IGotAnOffer: Anthropic software engineer interview (https://igotanoffer.com/en/advice/anthropic-software-engineer-interview)
OSTEP: Concurrency: An Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)

fields.Question: A service makes 5000 concurrent outbound HTTP calls that mostly wait on the network. Which model fits best?
fields.Choices:
One process per call
Exactly one thread per CPU core
Busy polling each socket in a loop
Async I/O on an event loop, or a pool of many lightweight threads
fields.Correct: Async I/O on an event loop, or a pool of many lightweight threads
fields.Explanation: I/O bound work spends its time waiting, so the goal is cheap concurrency, not more CPU. An event loop with epoll or many cheap threads handles thousands of waits. A process per call costs megabytes each and fork overhead. One thread per core caps in flight requests at the core count. Busy polling burns CPU doing nothing.
fields.Hint: Waiting is not computing.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Event-based Concurrency (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-events.pdf)
The C10K problem (http://www.kegel.com/c10k.html)

fields.Question: In an async server, one handler calls a blocking database driver (no await) that takes 2 seconds. What happens to other requests?
fields.Choices:
Only that request waits; the loop schedules others meanwhile
The runtime moves the blocking call to another core automatically
All of them stall for 2 seconds, because the event loop thread is blocked
The handler is cancelled after the loop's timeout
fields.Correct: All of them stall for 2 seconds, because the event loop thread is blocked
fields.Explanation: An event loop runs handlers on one thread and switches only at await points. A blocking call never yields, so nothing else runs until it returns. Offload it to a thread pool or use an async driver. The others assume preemption the loop does not do. Most loops have no automatic offload or default handler timeout.
fields.Hint: Where does the loop get control back?
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Event-based Concurrency (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-events.pdf)
IGotAnOffer: Anthropic software engineer interview (https://igotanoffer.com/en/advice/anthropic-software-engineer-interview)

fields.Question: What is the key difference between threads and processes for a crash in one worker?
fields.Choices:
Threads are isolated, so a crashing thread only ends itself
A crashing thread (for example a segfault) takes down the whole process; a crashing process does not affect others
Processes share memory, so one crash corrupts the others
There is no difference; the OS isolates both the same way
fields.Correct: A crashing thread (for example a segfault) takes down the whole process; a crashing process does not affect others
fields.Explanation: Threads share one address space, so a fatal signal from memory corruption kills every thread in the process. Separate processes have separate address spaces, which is why browsers and servers use process isolation. Thread isolation is the common misconception. Processes do not share memory unless they set it up explicitly.
fields.Hint: What is shared?
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Concurrency: An Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)
fork(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fork.2.html)

fields.Question: A multithreaded server calls fork() while another thread holds the malloc lock, and the child then calls malloc before exec. What can happen?
fields.Choices:
The child deadlocks, because only the forking thread exists in the child and the lock stays held forever
Nothing, the child gets copies of all threads, including the lock holder
The kernel releases all locks in the child
The child gets a fresh malloc state
fields.Correct: The child deadlocks, because only the forking thread exists in the child and the lock stays held forever
fields.Explanation: fork copies the whole address space but only the calling thread, so locks held by other threads are copied in the locked state with no owner left to release them. POSIX limits the child to async signal safe calls until exec. All threads being copied is the common wrong belief. The kernel knows nothing about user space locks. The heap is a copy of the parent's, lock included.
fields.Hint: How many threads does the child have?
fields.Source: fork(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fork.2.html)

fields.Question: A runtime multiplexes 100k lightweight tasks (goroutines, virtual threads) over a few OS threads. Which statement is true?
fields.Choices:
Each task gets its own core, so 100k tasks run in parallel
Shared data no longer needs synchronization
Blocking I/O inside a task always stalls every other task
Tasks are cheap to create and block, but CPU parallelism is still limited by the number of OS threads and cores
fields.Correct: Tasks are cheap to create and block, but CPU parallelism is still limited by the number of OS threads and cores
fields.Explanation: Lightweight tasks make concurrency cheap: small stacks and user space switching, with blocking calls parked on the runtime's poller. Parallel CPU work is still capped by cores. Tasks on different OS threads race on shared memory exactly like threads, so locks or channels are still needed. Modern runtimes park the task on I/O instead of stalling the OS thread, though some calls (pinned or native) can still block a carrier.
fields.Hint: Concurrency is not parallelism.
fields.Source:
The C10K problem (http://www.kegel.com/c10k.html)
OSTEP: Concurrency: An Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)

fields.Question: A job is 90% parallelizable and 10% strictly serial. What is the best possible speedup with unlimited cores?
fields.Choices:
90x
Unlimited, it scales with cores
10x
9x
fields.Explanation: Amdahl's law: speedup is at most 1 / serial fraction, here 1 / 0.1 = 10. Even infinite cores cannot shrink the serial 10%. 90x confuses the percentage with a speedup factor. Unlimited ignores the serial part. 9x would be the bound for about 11% serial.
fields.Hint: The serial part never shrinks.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Concurrency: An Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)

fields.Question: transfer(a, b) locks a then b. Two threads run transfer(x, y) and transfer(y, x) at the same time and hang. What is the standard fix?
fields.Choices:
Add a timeout to each lock acquire
Always lock the two accounts in a fixed order, such as by account id
Make the balances atomic integers
Lock a and b with a read lock instead
fields.Correct: Always lock the two accounts in a fixed order, such as by account id
fields.Explanation: Each thread holds one lock and waits for the other: circular wait. A global lock order breaks the cycle. Timeouts turn a deadlock into failures or livelock and still need retry logic. Atomic balances make each update safe but not the pair of updates. Read locks do not allow writes and both threads would still need the write lock.
fields.Hint: Break the circular wait.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)

fields.Question: Which condition, if removed, prevents deadlock and is the one most code actually removes?
fields.Choices:
Circular wait, by acquiring locks in a global order
Mutual exclusion, by removing locks
No preemption, by letting the OS take locks away
Hold and wait, by never using more than one thread
fields.Correct: Circular wait, by acquiring locks in a global order
fields.Explanation: All four Coffman conditions are needed for deadlock, so removing any one prevents it. Lock ordering removes circular wait and is cheap and local. Removing mutual exclusion means lock free code, which is hard. Preempting locks would leave data half updated. A single thread removes concurrency entirely, which is not a fix.
fields.Hint: There are four conditions; which is cheapest to break?
fields.Source: OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)

fields.Question: A cache lookup takes a mutex, and on a miss fetches from a remote service (100 ms) before releasing it. What is the main problem?
fields.Choices:
It deadlocks, because I/O cannot happen while holding a lock
It is fine, because the lock prevents duplicate fetches
The fetch result is lost when the lock is released
All lookups, including hits for other keys, queue behind the slow fetch
fields.Correct: All lookups, including hits for other keys, queue behind the slow fetch
fields.Explanation: Holding a lock across slow I/O serialises every caller for the duration, so throughput collapses to about 10 misses per second and even hits wait behind them. Fetch outside the lock with a per key in flight marker or future. I/O under a lock is legal, just slow. Preventing duplicate fetches does not require blocking every other key. Releasing a lock does not discard data.
fields.Hint: Who else needs this lock while you wait?
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)
SpaceComplexity: Databricks onsite interview (https://spacecomplexity.ai/blog/databricks-onsite-interview)

fields.Question:
Two threads call get_instance() at the same time with this code. What can go wrong?
if instance is None:
    instance = Expensive()
return instance
fields.Choices:
Nothing, assignment is atomic
A deadlock, since both wait on the constructor
Both can see None and construct two instances
The second thread waits automatically until the first finishes
fields.Correct: Both can see None and construct two instances
fields.Explanation: It is check then act: both threads pass the check before either assigns. Use a lock (with a re-check inside), or a language once primitive. Atomic assignment only means the pointer is not torn; it does not stop two constructions. There is no lock here, so no deadlock and no waiting.
fields.Hint: Check then act.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Concurrency: An Introduction (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: Double checked locking: check instance without the lock, lock, check again, construct and assign. In Java or C++, what extra requirement makes it correct?
fields.Choices:
Nothing, the second check inside the lock is enough
The instance field needs acquire and release semantics (volatile in Java, atomic in C++)
The constructor must be synchronized
The outer check must also take the lock
fields.Correct: The instance field needs acquire and release semantics (volatile in Java, atomic in C++)
fields.Explanation: Without ordering, the compiler or CPU can publish the pointer before the constructor's writes are visible, so the unlocked first check can return a half built object. Making the field volatile or atomic with release on store and acquire on load fixes it. The inner check prevents double construction, not unsafe publication. Synchronizing the constructor does not order the publish. Locking the outer check works but is just ordinary locking.
fields.Hint: The unlocked read can see a pointer before its contents.
fields.Source:
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)
What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory (https://people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdf)

fields.Question: Two threads each lock one resource, try lock the other, and on failure release and retry immediately. Both stay busy at 100% CPU but never finish. What is this and the usual fix?
fields.Choices:
Livelock; add randomized backoff before retrying, or use a global lock order
Deadlock; use try lock instead of lock
Starvation; raise the priority of one thread
A race condition; make the resources atomic
fields.Correct: Livelock; add randomized backoff before retrying, or use a global lock order
fields.Explanation: The threads are not blocked, they keep reacting to each other in lockstep, which is livelock. Random backoff breaks the symmetry, and lock ordering avoids the conflict entirely. It is not deadlock because nobody is waiting; they already use try lock. Starvation means one thread progresses while another never does. Atomic resources do not resolve the conflict over two locks.
fields.Hint: Busy but not progressing.
fields.Source: OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf)

fields.Question: A high priority task waits on a lock held by a low priority task, while a medium priority CPU bound task keeps preempting the low one. What is the standard fix?
fields.Choices:
Raise the medium task's priority
Make the high priority task spin instead of block
Increase the scheduler time slice
Priority inheritance: the lock holder temporarily runs at the waiter's priority
fields.Correct: Priority inheritance: the lock holder temporarily runs at the waiter's priority
fields.Explanation: This is priority inversion, the Mars Pathfinder bug. Priority inheritance boosts the low priority holder above the medium task so it finishes and releases the lock. Raising the medium task makes it worse. Spinning burns the CPU the holder needs. A longer slice does not stop priority preemption.
fields.Hint: Who must run for the high task to progress?
fields.Source: What really happened on Mars? (Glenn Reeves account) (https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs614/1999sp/papers/pathfinder.html)

fields.Question: A waiter checks a flag under a lock, releases the lock, and then calls wait on a condition variable. The setter takes the lock, sets the flag and signals. Sometimes the waiter sleeps forever. Why?
fields.Choices:
Condition variables need a timeout to work
The setter should signal before setting the flag
The signal can arrive between unlocking and waiting, and it is lost because condition variables have no memory
Two threads cannot share one condition variable
fields.Correct: The signal can arrive between unlocking and waiting, and it is lost because condition variables have no memory
fields.Explanation: Condition variable wait must atomically release the mutex and sleep, which is why it takes the mutex as an argument. Releasing it first opens a window where the signal fires with no one waiting and is dropped. A timeout masks the bug with latency. Signalling before setting makes it worse. Sharing a condition variable is its whole purpose.
fields.Hint: Why does wait take the mutex?
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Condition Variables (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-cv.pdf)
pthread_cond_wait, The Open Group Base Specifications (https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/pthread_cond_wait.html)

fields.Question: A thread pool with 16 workers and an unbounded task queue gets a burst it cannot keep up with for 10 minutes. What happens?
fields.Choices:
The pool adds threads automatically to keep up
The queue grows until memory runs out, and latency for queued tasks grows without limit
Extra tasks are rejected once the workers are busy
Throughput rises, since queued tasks are processed in batches
fields.Correct: The queue grows until memory runs out, and latency for queued tasks grows without limit
fields.Explanation: With an unbounded queue nothing pushes back, so arrivals above throughput pile up in memory and every new task waits behind the backlog. A bounded queue with a rejection policy, caller runs, or load shedding is backpressure. Many pools (Java ThreadPoolExecutor) only grow past core size when the queue is full, which never happens with an unbounded one. Rejection needs a bounded queue. Queuing adds latency, not throughput.
fields.Hint: What stops the producer?
fields.Source: Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: A pool runs tasks that spend 90% of their time waiting on network calls and 10% on CPU, on 8 cores. Roughly how many threads keep the CPUs busy?
fields.Correct: About 80
fields.Explanation: Threads needed is about cores times (1 + wait time / compute time) = 8 times (1 + 9) = 80. Eight threads would leave cores idle 90% of the time. Nine adds just one. Eight thousand wastes memory and adds switching while the CPUs are already saturated near 80.
fields.Hint: Cores times (1 + wait / compute).
fields.Source: Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: Tasks in a fixed pool of 4 threads submit a subtask to the same pool and block waiting for its result. Under load the service freezes. Why?
fields.Choices:
The pool's queue is not thread safe
Subtasks run on the caller thread and recurse forever
The futures were garbage collected before completion
All 4 threads are blocked waiting for subtasks that sit in the queue with no free thread to run them
fields.Correct: All 4 threads are blocked waiting for subtasks that sit in the queue with no free thread to run them
fields.Explanation: This is thread starvation deadlock: the parents occupy every worker, and the children they wait on cannot start. Use a separate pool for subtasks, avoid blocking (compose futures), or use a work stealing pool designed for fork and join. Executor queues are thread safe. A standard submit does not run the task on the caller. Pending futures are referenced by the queue.
fields.Hint: Who runs the subtask?
fields.Source: Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)

fields.Question: An ingest service reads from a client stream and hands records to a worker pool. Records must not be dropped, and memory must stay bounded. Which policy fits?
fields.Choices:
A bounded queue that drops the oldest record when full
An unbounded queue, since nothing is dropped
A bounded queue where the producer blocks when full, slowing reads from the client
A bounded queue that throws and discards the new record when full
fields.Correct: A bounded queue where the producer blocks when full, slowing reads from the client
fields.Explanation: Blocking the producer propagates backpressure upstream (TCP flow control slows the client), so nothing is lost and memory is capped. Dropping the oldest or the newest violates the no loss rule. An unbounded queue loses nothing until it exhausts memory, then loses everything.
fields.Hint: No drops and bounded memory leaves one option.
fields.Source:
Java Concurrency in Practice (https://jcip.net/)
The C10K problem (http://www.kegel.com/c10k.html)

fields.Question: A program calls write() and gets success, then the machine loses power one second later. Is the data guaranteed on disk?
fields.Choices:
Yes, a successful write means the data is on disk
No, write usually only copies into the page cache; fsync is needed to force it to stable storage
Yes, if the file was opened without O_APPEND
No, but closing the file would have guaranteed it
fields.Correct: No, write usually only copies into the page cache; fsync is needed to force it to stable storage
fields.Explanation: On Linux write returns once data is in the kernel page cache, which is flushed later. Only fsync, fdatasync or O_SYNC wait for the device. O_APPEND controls the offset, not durability. close does not flush to disk either; the man page says so explicitly.
fields.Hint: Where does write put the data?
fields.Source:
fsync(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fsync.2.html)
Ensuring data reaches disk (https://lwn.net/Articles/457667/)

fields.Question: You must replace config.json so that after a crash readers see either the old or the new file, and the new file must survive power loss once you report success. Which sequence is correct?
fields.Choices:
Write config.tmp, fsync it, rename it over config.json, then fsync the directory
Write config.tmp, rename it over config.json, then fsync config.json
Truncate config.json, write the new data, then fsync it
Write config.tmp, fsync it, then rename; rename is durable by itself
fields.Correct: Write config.tmp, fsync it, rename it over config.json, then fsync the directory
fields.Explanation: fsync of the temp file makes its contents durable before the name points at it, rename atomically swaps names, and fsync of the directory makes the new name durable. Renaming before fsync can leave a zero length or partial file after a crash on some file systems. Truncate then write has a window with no valid file. rename is atomic but not durable until the directory entry is flushed.
fields.Hint: Contents, name, then the directory.
fields.Source:
rename(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html)
Ensuring data reaches disk (https://lwn.net/Articles/457667/)
fsync(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fsync.2.html)

fields.Question: fsync returns EIO. The program retries fsync and it returns 0. On Linux, can it assume the data is durable?
fields.Choices:
Yes, the second fsync succeeded
Yes, the kernel keeps the pages dirty until a successful flush
Only if it reopens the file and fsyncs again
No, the failed dirty pages may have been dropped and marked clean, so the retry says nothing about that data
fields.Correct: No, the failed dirty pages may have been dropped and marked clean, so the retry says nothing about that data
fields.Explanation: After a writeback error Linux may discard or mark the affected pages clean and report the error once, so a later fsync returns success with the data gone. PostgreSQL changed to panic and recover from its WAL after this was found. The others all assume the kernel retains failed pages, which it does not promise. Reopening does not resurrect them.
fields.Hint: What happened to the pages that failed?
fields.Source:
Fsync Errors, PostgreSQL wiki (https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Fsync_Errors)
fsync(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fsync.2.html)

fields.Question: Design an LRU cache that survives a process crash and restart without losing acknowledged puts. What do you persist and when?
fields.Answer:
Log: append each put and delete to a write ahead log and fsync (or group commit several puts per fsync) before acknowledging.

Snapshot: periodically write the full map to a temp file, fsync, rename over the old snapshot, fsync the directory, then truncate the log.

Recovery: load the latest snapshot and replay the log; recency order can be rebuilt approximately from log order, since exact LRU order rarely needs durability.

Tradeoffs: fsync per put is slow, so batching trades a small loss window or latency for throughput; process crash alone is covered by the page cache, power loss needs fsync.
fields.Hint: Log before ack, snapshot with rename.
fields.Fact: A crash of the process and a loss of power need different guarantees.
fields.Source:
PracHub: Design a crash resilient LRU cache (https://prachub.com/interview-questions/design-a-crash-resilient-lru-cache)
OSTEP: Crash Consistency: FSCK and Journaling (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/file-journaling.pdf)
Ensuring data reaches disk (https://lwn.net/Articles/457667/)

fields.Question: Under load a server starts failing accept() and open() with EMFILE (too many open files), and the count slowly climbs over days. What is the most likely root cause?
fields.Choices:
The disk is full
A file descriptor leak, such as sockets or files not closed on an error path
The machine is out of RAM
Too many threads are running
fields.Correct: A file descriptor leak, such as sockets or files not closed on an error path
fields.Explanation: EMFILE means the process hit its RLIMIT_NOFILE descriptor limit, and a count that climbs over days points to descriptors not being closed. Check /proc/PID/fd to see what is leaking. Raising the limit only delays it. A full disk gives ENOSPC. Low memory gives ENOMEM or OOM kills. Threads do not consume descriptors by themselves.
fields.Hint: Which limit does EMFILE refer to?
fields.Source:
getrlimit(2), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/getrlimit.2.html)
proc(5), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc.5.html)

fields.Question: A process allocates 10 GB with malloc on a machine with 4 GB of RAM and malloc succeeds. Later the process is killed while writing to that memory. Why?
fields.Choices:
Linux overcommits: physical pages are assigned on first touch, and the OOM killer runs when they cannot be found
malloc reserved 10 GB of RAM, so another process caused the kill
The process hit a segfault because the pointer was invalid
The kernel swapped the memory and killed it for being slow
fields.Correct: Linux overcommits: physical pages are assigned on first touch, and the OOM killer runs when they cannot be found
fields.Explanation: With default overcommit, malloc reserves virtual address space only. Pages are backed on first write, and when RAM and swap run out the OOM killer picks a victim, often the biggest process. malloc did not reserve RAM. The pointer was valid; the kill is SIGKILL, not SIGSEGV. Swapping slows a process but the kernel does not kill for slowness.
fields.Hint: When does a page actually get RAM?
fields.Source:
Linux kernel docs: Overcommit Accounting (https://docs.kernel.org/mm/overcommit-accounting.html)
OSTEP: Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-beyondphys.pdf)

fields.Question: A Linux 8 core box shows load average 30 but CPU usage around 20%. What does that suggest?
fields.Choices:
The CPUs are overloaded nearly 4x
The load average is broken and should be ignored
There are 30 idle threads
Many tasks are blocked in uninterruptible I/O wait, such as on a slow disk or NFS, which Linux counts in load
fields.Correct: Many tasks are blocked in uninterruptible I/O wait, such as on a slow disk or NFS, which Linux counts in load
fields.Explanation: Linux load average counts runnable tasks plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (state D), usually disk or network file system I/O. With low CPU, the queue is waiting on I/O, not CPU. Treating load as pure CPU demand is the common mistake. The metric works, it just measures more than CPU. Idle threads sleeping interruptibly are not counted.
fields.Hint: Linux load includes more than CPU.
fields.Source:
Linux Load Averages: Solving the Mystery (https://www.brendangregg.com/blog/2017-08-08/linux-load-averages.html)
The USE Method (https://www.brendangregg.com/usemethod.html)

fields.Question: A service with 2000 threads on 8 cores spends much of its CPU time in the kernel, with very high context switch counts and low throughput. What is the best first fix?
fields.Choices:
Add more threads to hide the latency
Raise the scheduler time slice
Reduce the thread count, using a bounded pool or async I/O
Pin each thread to a core
fields.Correct: Reduce the thread count, using a bounded pool or async I/O
fields.Explanation: Far more runnable threads than cores means the scheduler constantly switches, paying for saving state and losing cache and TLB contents, and lock contention grows. A pool sized to the work removes most of it. More threads makes it worse. Time slice tuning does not help threads that block and wake frequently. You cannot pin 2000 threads to 8 cores usefully.
fields.Hint: Compare runnable threads to cores.
fields.Source:
Operating system interview questions (https://www.golinuxcloud.com/operating-system-interview-questions/)
OSTEP: Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs) (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-tlbs.pdf)

fields.Question: A latency sensitive service on a host near its memory limit shows p99 spikes that line up with a high rate of major page faults. What is happening?
fields.Choices:
The TLB is too small, which causes major faults
Pages are being read back from disk (swap or evicted file pages), so some memory accesses wait on I/O
The process uses too many threads
The CPU cache is thrashing between cores
fields.Correct: Pages are being read back from disk (swap or evicted file pages), so some memory accesses wait on I/O
fields.Explanation: A major fault needs disk I/O to bring a page in, so under memory pressure accesses to evicted pages take milliseconds instead of nanoseconds. Fix by reducing memory use, adding RAM, locking critical memory or tuning swap. TLB misses are handled by a page walk and are not page faults. Thread count does not cause major faults directly. Cache thrashing costs nanoseconds, not spikes visible at p99 in milliseconds.
fields.Hint: Major means the disk is involved.
fields.Source:
OSTEP: Beyond Physical Memory: Mechanisms (https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/vm-beyondphys.pdf)
proc(5), Linux manual page (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc.5.html)
